item.title: At least 32 killed in Ukraine, Zelenskiy condemns one of Russia's most 'vile strikes'
item.description: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes," President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said.
item.dc:creator: Olena Harmash, Vladyslav Smilianets
item.content:encoded: Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, killing at least 32 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure. The heaviest losses were in Pryluky in Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile destroyed a five-storey residential building. Ukraine's emergency service said on Telegram that the death toll in Pryluky has risen to 22 as of Thursday morning and two more bodies were discovered following a Russian air strike on an apartment building in the capital Kyiv, taking the toll there to four dead. Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi has earlier put the country-wide death toll at 28, including 20 people who died in the Pryluky attack, including five children. On Wednesday evening, prosecutors in Kyiv said falling debris from a drone killed two people in a suburb. Zelenskiy said that 100 people had been injured throughout the country. The president noted that the attacks coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday. "This is the kind of birthday present that Putin gave himself: the killing of children, the killing of people," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address. In earlier online comments, Zelenskiy said civilians had also been killed in the capital Kyiv and in the central cities of Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the massive attack. In total, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight — many of them high-velocity ballistic munitions — and dozens of Shahed attack drones, he said. "The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes." In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and brought out 15 survivors as they worked their way down through the rubble. Around 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said. "There's a lot of destruction, especially in the town centre," said Danylo Savenko, deputy mayor of Pryluky, who said he had run to an air raid shelter with his wife as soon as he heard the missiles flying. BIG JUMP IN REPORTED DRONE INTERCEPTIONS Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones. Ukraine's air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — an increase from recent weeks when air defences took down 50% to 60%. Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine's air defences struggling to cope. The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Zelenskiy said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were "every day looking for Patriot (missile interception) systems that can and must protect people's lives". Ukraine received a new €1.2 billion ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defence needs, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said. The US-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles. Global supplies have been drained by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict. Russia's defence ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defence company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv. Last week Zelenskiy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an [USN:L1N45R056 TEXT:"interview"] with Reuters, he said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow. PEOPLE SHELTER OVERNIGHT IN KYIV METRO Zelenskiy said Ukrainian troops hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions. In the Reuters interview, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would hit Russia's energy assets in response to Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure. Ukrainian officials and military intelligence shared warnings of the upcoming attacks on Wednesday, and many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city's underground metro stations. Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night. In the part of Ukraine's southern Kherson region under Russian control, the regional Russia-installed governor said a Ukrainian drone killed two civilians in a car. And Russia-installed officials in Moscow-held parts of eastern Donetsk Region said three people died in Ukrainian attacks. ($1 = 0.8947 euros)

item.title: India among seven countries vying for 2036 Olympics, IOC says
item.description: A shortlist will be drawn up in March next year and some countries will progress to a strategic dialogue phase.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Seven countries, including India, Germany and Qatar, are in the running to stage the 2036 Summer Olympics, the International Olympic Committee said on Tuesday. Hungary, Turkey, South Africa and South Korea complete the list of interested parties, who are in preliminary talks with the IOC, with a shortlist to be drawn up in March next year and some countries progressing to a strategic dialogue phase. "Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do ," said IOC President Kirsty Coventry. "That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point.” India, the world's most populous nation, is attempting to land its first Olympics while Qatar, which has bid before with Doha, is campaigning to become the first Muslim-majority nation to host the world's biggest multi-sports event. Qatar staged the 2022 soccer World Cup. Hungary, which most recently bid for the 2024 Olympics, has never staged the Games while Munich, host of the 1972 Olympics, is Germany's candidate. ISTANBUL TRIES AGAIN Turkey's Istanbul has failed in five previous attempts while South Africa is hoping to become the first African host of the Olympics. South Africa has major event experience, having organised the 2010 soccer World Cup. South Korea has staged both summer and winter Olympics in Seoul in 1988 and Pyeongchang in 2018. Preferred hosts will be named after the dialogue phase in 2028 and a final decision is expected in mid-2029. Any other interested countries have until October 31 to come forward but new candidates are highly unlikely to emerge with less than four weeks before the deadline. Bidding rules changed under Coventry this year, adding the strategic dialogue stage and involving members more throughout the process. It is also very likely that more than one country will be named as preferred hosts, unlike in past votes where just one bidder was put forward by the IOC executive board. Los Angeles will stage the 2028 Summer Games and Australia's Brisbane will host them four years later.

item.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
item.description: The scientist won for his work creating an observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos.
item.dc:creator: Niklas Pollard, Johan Ahlander, Marie Mannes
item.content:encoded: The Belgian-American scientist Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work creating an Antarctic observatory of ice to detect high-energy neutrinos, elusive subatomic particles that can reveal otherwise inaccessible information about the cosmos. Halzen, 82, realised that pristine ice at the South Pole could be used to track such neutrinos, sometimes known as "ghost particles" for the way they pass through the Earth without a trace, only interacting with matter extremely rarely. "The messengers bring information from the cosmos," Eva Olsson, of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, told a press conference. "They open the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars." "It's a great relief for me because this was not totally unexpected, and around this time of the year I always felt miserable because I didn't win the prize and thought it was terrible for my collaborators who deserved it so much," Halzen said at a press conference. "So that problem is finally solved." HALZEN HAILED FOR DETECTING 'MESSENGERS FROM THE COSMOS' The interactions registered by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory provide information about how high-energy particles are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said. "We could catch them in ice, that was the goal," Halzen said of the years-long effort to construct the observatory, which he described as opening "a window on the universe." In 2014, the US-based Smithsonian magazine dubbed Halzen "Neutrino Man" when giving him one of its Ingenuity Awards, acclaiming him for an "amazing experiment (that) heralds the beginning of a new era in astronomy". It even published a comic illustrating his life: "How One Physicist's Pursuit of the Cosmos Took Off in Antarctica". The observatory – in effect a telescope that shows neutrinos instead of light – is set in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, which extends to a depth of 2,500 metres below the surface near the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. More than 5,000 sensors await blips from the nearly massless high-energy neutrinos, which unlike other particles do not lose energy or change direction, in the hope of tracing their paths back to exploding stars, gamma-ray bursts, and cataclysmic phenomena involving black holes and neutron stars. They can expect to register about one per day. Halzen, a professor at the University of Wisconsin–Madison in the US, first presented his idea in 1988 for capturing neutrino traces at the South Pole, but the project was not completed until 2011. "I have to emphasise how lucky I was because, when we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea, but very few thought it would work, including myself," Halzen told the press conference by telephone. Neutrinos are electrically neutral, undisturbed by any magnetic field, which means that, in contrast to electromagnetic waves such as visible light, the direction from which they arrive points directly back to their source. FRUITS OF HALZEN'S RESEARCH YET TO COME The observatory has determined that high-energy neutrinos originate within but also far outside our own Milky Way galaxy, setting in motion an interstellar quest to find the objects and processes that create them. Through the long winter at the South Pole, when bringing anything in or out is difficult as temperatures below minus 50 degrees Celsius (minus 58 Fahrenheit) preclude even aircraft landing, a skeleton crew of "winterovers" has to maintain the observatory. The station, home to many other activities, can house as many as 150 people and has an industrial kitchen, dining room, gym and even a greenhouse. Last week it celebrated the sun's return above the horizon after six months of night with a six-hole ice-golf tournament. An extension, IceCube-Gen2, encompassing 8 cubic kilometres of ice, is planned to become operational in 2033 and will be able to detect 10 times as many neutrinos, including much weaker ones. Halzen said the main fruits of his work were yet to be seen and that it was too early to say exactly what it could reveal about the universe. "This is a new way of looking at the universe, and it will take bigger telescopes, many more telescopes, to become real astronomy," he said. "And what this will bring is impossible to predict." WINNERS FROM EINSTEIN TO BOHR AND THE CURIES Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever congratulated Halzen on the recognition of "a life dedicated to unraveling the greatest secrets of the cosmos through its most minuscule manifestations". The physics laureate [USN:L8N45A0P9 TEXT:"receives"] an award of 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million). Past winners include several other neutrino research pioneers, for instance Japan's Takaaki Kajita and Arthur McDonald from Canada in 2015. The [USN:L1N45R0AK TEXT:"Nobel Prizes"] were [USN:L1N45N0AY TEXT:"established"] under the will of Swedish inventor and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, whose fortune was built in part on the invention of dynamite. Physics was prominent in Nobel's will and the prize remains one of the discipline's highest distinctions. Over the decades, it has recognised discoveries that have fundamentally reshaped humanity's understanding of the universe. Among past laureates are some of the most celebrated figures in science, including Albert Einstein, Marie and Pierre Curie, Max Planck and Niels Bohr, whose work helped establish the foundations of modern physics. The prize is presented in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death. ($1 = 10.0329 Swedish crowns)

item.title: Qualcomm and Arm kick off trial, potential for huge damages in focus
item.description: Chipmaker Qualcomm and chip tech firm Arm Holdings , , long at loggerheads, began another trial on Monday, with Qualcomm accusing Arm of withholding chip testing tools that were due under contract.
item.dc:creator: Tom Hals, Max Cherney, Stephen Nellis
item.content:encoded: (This Oct 5 has been corrected to say that Arm was seeking an 18,500% increase in royalty rates, not 1,800%, in paragraph 10.) Chipmaker Qualcomm (QCOM.O) and chip tech firm Arm Holdings (O9Ty.F) , , long at loggerheads, began another trial on Monday, with Qualcomm accusing Arm of withholding chip testing tools that were due under contract. Qualcomm also alleges that Arm leaked to the media its 2024 threat to terminate [USN:L4N3LZ01S TEXT:"a vital license agreement"] in a way that damaged discussions for a chip deal between Qualcomm and Meta Platforms (META.O) . In the lawsuit brought before US federal court in Delaware, Qualcomm, one of Arm's largest customers, is seeking to quit paying royalties — potentially worth billions of dollars — to Arm for up to five years. Qualcomm attorney Karen Dunn said in her opening statement that Qualcomm had been on the cusp of a deal with Meta when Arm notified Qualcomm that it was in breach of its architecture agreement and then allegedly leaked that notification letter to Bloomberg News. Meta became concerned Qualcomm would lose its license and Dunn told the jury that by the time Qualcomm secured the Meta deal the value had decreased by $170 million. “Delay is costly,” she told the jury. But Arm's attorney Gregg LoCascio told the jury it would learn that what really happened is Meta shifted to AI eyeglasses and away from virtual reality headsets and sought to adjust financial terms for Qualcomm chips as a result. “They were not harmed in the least,” LoCascio said. While a five-year hold on royalty payments sought by Qualcomm could be a major sales impact for Arm, Judge Maryellen Noreika is weighing whether to throw out that term of the contract, which could mean Qualcomm would be able to seek only a smaller amount of damages. In a related bench trial, Noreika also heard arguments over whether Arm has negotiated in good faith with Qualcomm for the next version of Arm's chip technology. Qualcomm's agreement with Arm runs through 2033. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon testified during the bench trial portion of Monday's proceedings, during which Qualcomm's attorney returned repeatedly to a chart that showed Arm was seeking an increase of 18,500% in its royalty payments between version 9 and version 10 of its computing architecture. During a cross-examination, Arm's attorney pressed Amon on whether Qualcomm was aiming to get Arm to stick to pricing in a 2013 architecture licensing deal that capped royalties at $1.88 per chip for any chip with at least five central processor cores. Arm’s attorney asked Amon whether that agreement, which dates from an era of smaller smartphone chips, was under-priced in 2026’s market, where some data center chips have 288 central processor cores. The attorney asked Amon if the deal structure means that Qualcomm would be paying royalties for five central processor cores on larger chips and “getting 283 for free.” Amon responded that “I don’t see it that way.” The five-day trial marks another stage in the contentious relationship between Arm and Qualcomm. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022 alleging that Qualcomm had breached its contracts, though Qualcomm came away in 2024 with a [USN:L1N3NL0WF TEXT:"key victory"].

item.title: OFRBS Summary
item.description: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Les valeurs à suivre à Paris et en Europe Les valeurs à suivre jeudi à la Bourse de Paris et en Europe : Zone euro: Les ventes au détail rebondissent moins que prévu en août 6 octobre (Reuters) - Les ventes au détail dans la zone euro ont rebondi légèrement moins que prévu sur un mois en août, selon les données publiées mardi par Eurostat, l'office statistique de l'Union européenne. Allemagne: Baisse surprise des exportations en août 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les exportations allemandes ont baissé de façon inattendue en août, accusant un recul de 0,8% par rapport au mois précédent, selon les données de l'Office fédéral de la statistique publiées jeudi. Etats-Unis: Les responsables de la Fed divisés sur la justification de la hausse des taux-"minutes" WASHINGTON, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Les responsables de la Réserve fédérale (Fed) ont divergé le mois dernier sur le raisonnement justifiant de relever les taux d'intérêt, certains d'entre eux notant la nécessité de contrer le choc énergétique tandis que d'autres, plus conservateurs, ayant dit avant tout vouloir lutter contre l'inflation. FORVIA HELLA décroche deux commandes majeures pour ses solutions EnergyCore 8 octobre (Reuters) - FORVIA a annoncé jeudi que sa filiale FORVIA HELLA avait remporté deux importantes commandes en série pour ses solutions EnergyCore pour un montant cumulé "dans la fourchette des centaines de millions d'euros". Samsung anticipe un bénéfice du T3 en hausse de 783% SÉOUL, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Samsung Electronics a déclaré jeudi que son bénéfice d'exploitation au troisième trimestre devrait bondir de 783% sur un an, battant les attentes des analystes, en raison d'une forte demande liée à l'intelligence artificielle (IA). Estanguet et Musca nommés au conseil d'administration de Christian Dior PARIS, 7 octobre (Reuters) - L'ancien champion olympique de canoë-kayak, Tony Estanguet, et Xavier Musca ont été nommés au conseil d'administration de Christian Dior, en remplacement de Nicolas Bazire et Maria Luisa Loro Piana, a annoncé le couturier français mercredi dans un communiqué. La Fondation Rockefeller propose un plan pour relancer la croissance des pays en développement endettés WASHINGTON, 7 octobre (Reuters) - La Fondation Rockefeller et ses partenaires ont dévoilé mercredi une initiative visant à aider les pays en développement fortement endettés à accéder à de nouveaux financements afin de stimuler leur croissance économique. Opmobility baisse ses objectifs 2026 à cause du marché auto, 770 emplois supprimés 7 octobre (Reuters) - L'équipementier automobile français OPmobility a annoncé mardi une révision à la baisse de ses objectifs 2026 et des projets de réorganisation qui entraîneraient la suppression d'environ 770 postes en France et en Allemagne, face à une dégradation du marché plus marquée que prévu. France: Le déficit commercial s'établit à €6,122 milliards à fin août 7 octobre(Reuters) - Le déficit commercial de la France s'est établi à 6,122 milliards d'euros à fin août, montrent les données publiées mercredi par le bureau des Douanes françaises.

item.title: OFRMO Summary
item.description: Le bilan de la vaste attaque russe en Ukraine mercredi passe à 32 morts
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Le bilan de la vaste attaque russe en Ukraine mercredi passe à 32 morts KYIV, 8 octobre (Reuters) - Le bilan de la pluie de missiles et de drones russes qui s'est abattue sur l'Ukraine dans la nuit de mardi à mercredi est passé à 32 morts et 100 blessés après le décès de deux personnes tuées par des débris de drones mercredi soir dans une banlieue de Kyiv. Un Palestinien tué dans une attaque de colons pendant la récolte des olives, selon les autorités BURQA, Cisjordanie, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Un Palestinien a été tué mercredi lors d'une attaque menée par des colons israéliens dans une oliveraie près du village de Burqa, en Cisjordanie occupée par Israël, a annoncé le ministère palestinien de la Santé. La Syrie envisage d'aider militairement Ryad, selon des sources RYAD, 8 octobre (Reuters) - La Syrie, proche alliée de l'Arabie saoudite, envisage de fournir une assistance militaire à Ryad dans la guerre au Yémen contre les Houthis, ont déclaré un responsable américain et une source militaire syrienne. Etats-Unis/Midterms: Trump au Texas, bastion républicain où le scrutin s'annonce serré SAN ANTONIO, Texas, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Le président américain Donald Trump s'est rendu mercredi au Texas pour la troisième fois en un mois afin de faire campagne en faveur des républicains, qui se retrouvent engagés dans des scrutins de mi-mandat plus serrés que prévu. Les Houthis disent avoir lancé un missile balistique contre un aéroport de Ryad 8 octobre (Reuters) - Les rebelles houthis du Yémen ont déclaré jeudi avoir lancé un missile balistique contre l'aéroport King Khalid de Ryad, en Arabie saoudite. Japon: Les soldats américains soumis à un couvre-feu à Okinawa après une affaire de meurtre TOKYO, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Les soldats américains stationnés à Okinawa, au Japon, se sont vu imposer un couvre-feu d'un mois et un stage de discipline, suspendant les opérations militaires sur place, après qu'un marine a été accusé d’avoir assassiné et dérobé une femme de la région. Israël commémore le 7-Octobre, trois ans après JERUSALEM, 7 octobre (Reuters) - Israël a commémoré mercredi les attaques du Hamas survenues sur son territoire le 7 octobre 2023, le jour le plus meurtrier de son histoire dont le souvenir pèse sur la campagne des élections législatives prévues dans moins de trois semaines. L'OMS demande plus d'informations à Moscou sur le décès d'une employée d'un institut dédié à la peste 7 octobre (Reuters) - L'Organisation mondiale de la santé a déclaré mercredi avoir demandé à la Russie davantage d'informations sur les causes du décès d'une employée d'un institut spécialisé dans la peste en Sibérie, soulignant que la transparence était essentielle pour se faire une idée précise des risques sanitaires potentiels. L'Iran doit réduire ses activités d'enrichissement d'uranium pour mettre fin à la guerre, dit Vance Le vice-président américain J.D. Vance a déclaré dans une interview accordée à Reuters que l'Iran réduire de manière "significative" sa capacité d'enrichissement nucléaire pour satisfaire aux exigences des Etats-Unis et mettre fin à la guerre. Des marins disparus en mer Noire après une frappe de drone sur leur navire au large de la Bulgarie L'équipage d'un navire marchand est porté disparu après que leur bateau a coulé à la suite d'une attaque de drone subie pendant qu'il naviguait dans la zone économique bulgare de la mer Noire, a déclaré le Premier ministre bulgare, Rouman Radev, qualifiant l'incident de violation flagrante du droit international.
